approachQuestion.prompt:
Archive Ordering
Sort a mutable array of n signed integers into nondecreasing order in the same array. Preserve duplicates. A stable order among equal values is not required. Example: [4,1,4,−2] → [−2,1,4,4].

0 ≤ n ≤ 200000; signed 32-bit values. Require a worst-case comparison bound and constant auxiliary space, including call stacks. No second array may be allocated. Which approach best meets this contract?
constraints: 0 ≤ n ≤ 200000; signed 32-bit values. Require a worst-case comparison bound and constant auxiliary space, including call stacks. No second array may be allocated.

options.text: Build a max-heap in place using bottom-up iterative sift-down. Swap its root with the last active element, shrink the active prefix, and repair only that prefix. Repeat until at most one active element remains.
options.feedback: Each maximum moves to its final position at the front of a growing sorted suffix. Excluding that suffix from repair preserves values already finalized.

options.text: Build a min-heap in place, then repeatedly swap its root to the last active position and shrink the prefix, without reversing afterward.
options.feedback: This places successive minima at the right and gives descending order; [2,1] finishes [2,1].

options.text: Use recursive quicksort with the first element as pivot and ordinary two-way partitioning, without any fallback.
options.feedback: Sorted distinct input repeatedly leaves one subproblem almost as large as the original. This misses the requested worst-case comparison guarantee and can retain a linear call stack.

options.text: Use the max-heap procedure, but after each root swap restore heap order over the entire n-element array.
options.feedback: The finalized maximum reenters the heap. For [2,1], restoring the whole max-heap after the swap gives [2,1] again, which is unsorted.

After moving the maximum to the end, exclude that sorted suffix from all later repairs. The active prefix remains a heap. Iterative sifting avoids both a helper heap and a recursion stack.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze A: iterative bottom-up max-heap construction followed by shrinking-prefix root exchanges and iterative repairs. Let n be length. The input array is also the final output; no copies or recursive calls are made. Choose the tightest time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Use the tightest worst-case bound for the whole input unless amortized or expected accounting is explicitly specified. Comparing or moving a record and arithmetic on machine words take constant time.

Exclude supplied input and returned output from auxiliary space. Count working arrays, queues, tables and call stacks. Output storage is separate and is not used as workspace. Heap repairs and traversals are iterative. No hashing is used unless explicitly stated.

options.text: O(n log(n+1)) time, O(1) auxiliary space
O(n log(n+1)) time, O(n) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Linear heap construction is followed by logarithmic removals from shrinking prefixes.
details: Construction is O(n). A linear number of removals may traverse logarithmic active heights; summed across shrinking prefixes this is O(n log(n+1)), with comparison-sorting inputs attaining the bound. Swaps and iterative repair keep only constant state. Reusing the supplied array is allowed, and no separate output copying is needed.
“O(n) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Heap construction alone is linear; extraction and sorting are not.
“O(n log(n+1)) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: No auxiliary heap or copied output is allocated.
“O(n²) time, O(log(n+1)) auxiliary space”: This is not unprotected recursive quicksort; shrinking-heap repairs have a logarithmic bound.
